  one-off loss spikes              aberrant batch, lr near the edge of 2/L (thm. 3.1)                 inspect the data, lower the lr, gradient clipping
  exploding gradient norm          poorly conditioned recurrences (ch. 5)                             clip $\|\hat g\|$ to a threshold (standard: 1.0)
  train goes down, val stagnates   overfitting                                                        ch. 3.6, in order of payoff
  neither train nor val moves      lr too small, blockage (dead ReLUs), loss mis-wired                LR range test, per-layer activation statistics

Tools: tensorboard/wandb; systematically log the loss, accuracy, gradient norm, weight norm, the fraction of zero activations (dying ReLU), and the activation histograms of a few layers.

### 8.3. GPU: the levers that matter

-   **Mixed precision** (bf16 preferably): \~2× throughput, memory divided by \~2 — the first reflex (ch. 2).
-   **Batch and accumulation**: saturate the GPU (measure utilization); if memory runs out, accumulate small batches; adjust the BatchNorm statistics accordingly.
-   **DataLoader**: workers > 0, pin_memory, prefetch — a GPU waiting for data is a wasted GPU (CPU preprocessing is often the real bottleneck).
-   **torch.compile**, fused kernels (FlashAttention, ch. 6), avoid CPU→GPU synchronizations inside the loop (the .item() / prints at each step).

### 8.4. Reproducibility

```python
import torch, numpy as np, random

def seed_everything(seed=42):
    random.seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)

seed_everything(42)
torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True    # determinism (speed cost)
torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False       # disable non-deterministic autotuning
```

Set the seeds (python/numpy/torch/cuda), the data shuffling, and record the library versions; some CUDA kernels remain non-deterministic by nature (atomics); aim for reproducibility *up to a tolerance* rather than bit-for-bit, and document configurations and seeds in every experiment. Reproducibility is also a debugging tool: a random bug you know how to reproduce is half fixed.

## 9. Generative models: AE, VAE, GAN, diffusion {#ch9}

The networks of the previous chapters predict a label $y$ from an input $x$; a generative model learns the distribution of $x$ itself, so that it can produce new images or sentences. This chapter compares four ways of doing so — autoencoders, variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks and diffusion models — derives the training objective of each, and codes a VAE and a small diffusion model.

### 9.1. Deterministic autoencoder and its pathology

An autoencoder compresses $x$ into a code $z = E_\phi(x)$ and reconstructs $\hat x = D_\theta(z)$, trained on $\|x - \hat x\|^2$. Useful for representation learning though it is, it is not a *generative* model: the latent space has no imposed structure — sampling $z$ at random gives aberrant reconstructions. The VAE corrects precisely this.

::: note
[Linear autoencoder and PCA (Baldi & Hornik, 1989)]{.tag} Take centred data, a linear encoder $z = W_e x$ with $W_e \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$, a linear decoder $\hat x = W_d z$ and the squared reconstruction error.

The map $x \mapsto W_d W_e x$ has rank at most $k$, so by the Eckart–Young theorem the best achievable error is that of the projection onto the top $k$ principal directions, and every global minimizer reconstructs through exactly that projection (when $\lambda_k > \lambda_{k+1}$). The weights themselves are identified only up to an invertible $k \times k$ change of basis of the code.

A linear autoencoder is thus PCA (Machine Learning module, section 7.3) learned by gradient descent; nonlinear encoders and decoders extend dimensionality reduction to curved data, and a *denoising* autoencoder, which reconstructs $x$ from a corrupted copy, learns features that are robust to that corruption.
:::

### 9.2. VAE: the ELBO fully derived

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2013)]{.tag} Diagonal Gaussian encoder
$$
q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\phi(x), \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x))\big),
$$
decoder $p_\theta(x \mid z)$, prior $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. One maximizes the **ELBO** (evidence lower bound):
$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi; x) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0, I)\big).
$$
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.2 — Exact decomposition of the log-likelihood]{.tag} $$\log p_\theta(x) = \mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi; x) + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\big\|\,p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) \;\ge\; \mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi; x).$$ Maximizing the ELBO = maximizing a lower bound of $\log p_\theta(x)$ *and* bringing $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ closer to the exact posterior $p_\theta(z \mid x)$.
:::

::: proof
Start from the definition of the KL between $q_\phi(\cdot \mid x)$ and the posterior $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)$, both over $z$ (at fixed $x$), and expand with $p_\theta(x, z) = p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)$ (Bayes):
$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi \| p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\big) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(z)] + \log p_\theta(x).
$$
Now, by definition of the KL against the prior,
$$
\mathbb{E}_q[\log q] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(z)] = \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| \mathcal{N}(0,I)).
$$
Substituting:
$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi \| p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\big) = \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| \mathcal{N}) - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] + \log p_\theta(x),
$$
that is, rearranging:
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| \mathcal{N})}_{=\ \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x)} + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi \| p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\big).
$$
The KL is nonnegative (Jensen applied to $\mathbb{E}_q[\log(q/p)] \ge -\log \mathbb{E}_q[p/q] = 0$), giving the bound. Equality iff $q_\phi(z \mid x) = p_\theta(z \mid x)$ exactly. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Reading the proof]{.tag} One cannot optimize $\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz$ directly: the integral is intractable. The ELBO is the only quantity that requires only (i) *samples* from $q_\phi$ (Monte Carlo: a single one suffices in practice) and (ii) a *closed-form* KL. It is the same trade-off as in EM (Machine Learning module): the residual KL measures exactly what the bound loses.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.3 — Reparameterization: why $z = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon$ works]{.tag} If $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and $z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon$, then
$$
z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x)))
$$
*and*
$$
\nabla_\phi \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[f(z)] = \mathbb{E}_\varepsilon\big[\nabla_\phi f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \odot \varepsilon)\big]:
$$
the gradient gets through. Sampling $z \sim q_\phi$ directly blocks the gradient (the sampling operation has no derivative with respect to its parameters).
:::

::: proof
The law of $z$ is obtained by an affine change of variable, whose Jacobian
$$
\partial z/\partial \varepsilon = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma)
$$
is constant: the density of $z$ is that of a Gaussian with mean $\mu$, covariance $\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2)$.

For the gradient: the expectation under $q_\phi$ rewrites as an expectation under the *fixed* law of $\varepsilon$,
$$
\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[f(z)] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \odot \varepsilon)];
$$
the distribution is *no longer* parameterized by $\phi$ — $\phi$ now appears only in the integrand, which gradient descent knows how to differentiate (theorem 2.1). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.4 — Closed-form KL between diagonal Gaussians]{.tag} For $q = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2))$ and $p = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ in dimension $k$: $$\mathrm{KL}(q \| p) = \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^{k} \big(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_i^2\big).$$
:::

::: proof
$\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q(z) - \log p(z)]$. Coordinate by coordinate (the densities factorize), with $\varphi$ the standard Gaussian density:
$$
\log q(z_i) - \log \varphi(z_i) = -\tfrac12\log\sigma_i^2 - \frac{(z_i - \mu_i)^2}{2\sigma_i^2} + \frac{z_i^2}{2}.
$$
Under $q$, $z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma_i^2)$, so $\mathbb{E}_q[(z_i - \mu_i)^2] = \sigma_i^2$ and $\mathbb{E}_q[z_i^2] = \mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2$. Taking the expectation:
$$
-\tfrac12\log\sigma_i^2 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac12(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2),
$$
that is $\tfrac12(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_i^2)$.

Along the way one checks that each term is $\ge 0$, zero iff $\mu_i = 0, \sigma_i = 1$ (study of $u - 1 - \log u \ge 0$). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[The ELBO trade-off in practice]{.tag} First term: reconstruction. Second: a regularizer that keeps the codes close to the prior — too strong, everything blurs together (codes ignored, blurry sampling); too weak, the latent space develops "holes" (partial posterior collapse). The connection with variational inference and EM is taken up again in the Machine Learning module; the extensions ($\beta$-VAE, VQ-VAE) are in Multimodal Generative AI.
:::

The lab of session 11 codes the whole section in about twenty lines: the Gaussian encoder, the reparameterization of proposition 9.3, the closed-form KL of proposition 9.4 and a Bernoulli decoder, whose negative log-likelihood is the binary cross-entropy on the pixels.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=784, h=400, k=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc, self.mu, self.logvar = nn.Linear(d, h), nn.Linear(h, k), nn.Linear(h, k)
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(k, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, d))
    def forward(self, x):
        e = F.relu(self.enc(x))
        mu, logvar = self.mu(e), self.logvar(e)
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)   # reparameterization (prop. 9.3)
        return self.dec(z), mu, logvar                             # decoder logits

def neg_elbo(x, logits, mu, logvar):          # minus the ELBO, in nats per image
    rec = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, x, reduction="sum")  # -log p(x|z), Bernoulli pixels
    kl = 0.5 * (mu**2 + logvar.exp() - 1 - logvar).sum()                 # proposition 9.4
    return (rec + kl) / len(x)

torch.manual_seed(0)
data = datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(data, batch_size=128, shuffle=True)
model = VAE(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for epoch in range(10):
    for x, _ in loader:
        x = x.view(-1, 784)
        loss = neg_elbo(x, *model(x))
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    print(epoch, round(loss.item(), 1))       # last batch: ~129 nats after epoch 0, ~105 after epoch 9
with torch.no_grad():                         # generation: decode z ~ N(0, I)
    samples = torch.sigmoid(model.dec(torch.randn(64, 16))).view(64, 28, 28)
```

### 9.3. GAN: the minimax game and its equilibrium

::: def
[Definition 9.5 — GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014)]{.tag} Minimax game between a generator $G$ (often $G(z)$ with $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$) and a discriminator $D : \mathcal{X} \to (0,1)$: $$\min_G \max_D \ V(G, D), \qquad V(G, D) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}\big[\log(1 - D(G(z)))\big].$$
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.6 — Optimal discriminator and global equilibrium]{.tag}

1.  For fixed $G$, the maximand reads (with $p_G$ the law of $G(z)$)
    $$
    V(G,D) = \int \big[p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\log D(x) + p_G(x) \log(1 - D(x))\big] dx,
    $$
    maximized pointwise at
    $$
    D^\star(x) = \frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x) + p_G(x)}.
    $$
2.  The value of the game is then
    $$
    V(G, D^\star) = -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\mathrm{data}} \| p_G),
    $$
    minimized over $G$ exactly when $p_G = p_{\mathrm{data}}$: the global equilibrium exists and coincides with the law of the data.
:::

::: proof
**1)** For each fixed $x$, maximize $a\log D + b\log(1-D)$ with $a = p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)$, $b = p_G(x)$.

The derivative $a/D - b/(1-D) = 0$ gives $D^\star = a/(a+b)$ (strict concavity in $D \in (0,1)$).

**2)** Rewrite
$$
\log D^\star = \log \frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{p_{\mathrm{data}}+p_G} = \log\frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{m} - \log 2
$$
and
$$
\log(1 - D^\star) = \log \frac{p_G}{m} - \log 2,
$$
where $m = \frac12(p_{\mathrm{data}} + p_G)$. Then
$$
V(G, D^\star) = \int p_{\mathrm{data}} \log\frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{m} + \int p_G \log\frac{p_G}{m} - 2\log 2 = 2\,\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\mathrm{data}} \| p_G) - \log 4,
$$
by definition of the Jensen–Shannon divergence (average of the KLs toward $m$).

Since $\mathrm{JSD} \ge 0$ with equality if and only if $p_{\mathrm{data}} = p_G$ almost everywhere (each KL toward the mixture $m$ vanishes only when the law equals $m$), the minimum $-\log 4$ is reached exactly at equilibrium.

**Gaussian case**: if $p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(\mu_d, \sigma_d^2)$ and $G(z) = \mu + \sigma z$, then $p_G = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and the equilibrium corresponds to the exact parameters $(\mu, \sigma) = (\mu_d, \sigma_d)$.

The logit of $D^\star$, $\log p_{\mathrm{data}} - \log p_G$, is a degree-2 polynomial in $x$ — a quadratic discriminator suffices. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Why it is unstable nonetheless]{.tag} The theorem describes the equilibrium, not the *dynamics*: the two players descend their gradients *simultaneously*, and if $D$ becomes too good too fast, the gradient of $G$ vanishes ($\log(1 - D)$ saturates). Emblematic pathology: **mode collapse** — $G$ concentrates on the "easiest" modes of $p_{\mathrm{data}}$ (a few very credible faces instead of all of them).

Historical remedies: Wasserstein-GAN (transportation distance instead of JSD — cf. Optimal Transport module), gradient penalization, feature matching. In imaging, the family was superseded by **diffusion** (iterative denoising, section 9.4): Ye Zhu's models (chapter 10) are recent developments of it, and the Multimodal Generative AI module treats them in detail.

LLMs, for their part, remain autoregressive: $\mathbb{P}(x_t \mid x_{<t})$, cross-entropy loss over tokens (LLMs module, M2).
:::

### 9.4. Diffusion in one page {#diffusion}

A GAN generates in one shot and pays with an unstable game; a VAE is stable but its samples are blurry. Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020) take a third route: destroy the data with noise in many small steps, and train a network to undo one step at a time.

Each step is a plain regression, so training is as stable as supervised learning; the price is paid at sampling time.

::: def
[Definition 9.7 — Forward (noising) process]{.tag} Choose a schedule $0 < \beta_1 < \dots < \beta_T < 1$, and set $\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t$ and $\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}\alpha_s$. Starting from a data point $x_0$, each step shrinks the signal and adds Gaussian noise:
$$
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\big).
$$
Nothing is learned in this process.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.8 — Closed form of the forward process]{.tag} For every $t$,
$$
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_t)\, I\big), \qquad\text{that is}\qquad x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).
$$
:::

::: proof
By induction on $t$; the case $t = 1$ is the definition. Assume
$$
x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\varepsilon' .
$$
Then
$$
x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\,\varepsilon_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}\,\varepsilon' + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t}\,\varepsilon_t .
$$
The last two terms are independent centred Gaussians, so their sum is Gaussian with variance
$$
\alpha_t(1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}) + 1 - \alpha_t = 1 - \bar\alpha_t .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

Two consequences. Any noise level is sampled in one step, without simulating the chain.

And with the schedule of Ho et al. ($T = 1\,000$, $\beta_t$ rising linearly from $10^{-4}$ to $0.02$), the sum of the $\beta_t$ is about $10$ and
$$
\bar\alpha_T \approx 4 \times 10^{-5}:
$$
$x_T$ is pure noise to excellent accuracy, which is where sampling starts.

A network $\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ receives the noisy point and the step, and is trained to predict the noise that was added:

::: key
[Key result — the noise-prediction loss]{.tag}
$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\ t \sim \mathcal{U}\{1, \dots, T\},\ \varepsilon}\,\big\|\varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\ t\big)\big\|^2 .
$$
:::

Ho et al. show that the ELBO of section 9.2, written for the whole chain, is, up to a constant and a final reconstruction term, a sum of KL divergences between Gaussians, each a weighted squared error on $\varepsilon$; dropping the weights gives this loss, which trains better. The derivation is in [Multimodal Generative AI ch. 3](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch3).

::: thm
[Algorithm 9.9 — Ancestral sampling]{.tag} Draw $x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. For $t = T, \dots, 1$, draw $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ (and set $z = 0$ at the last step), then
$$
x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\Big) + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, z .
$$
The first term removes the predicted noise; the second re-injects a little fresh noise, which keeps the chain a sampler rather than a deterministic denoiser.
:::

**Cost.** One network evaluation per step: $T = 1\,000$ forward passes per sample, against one for a VAE or a GAN. Deterministic samplers (DDIM) bring this down to a few tens of steps, and distillation to a handful ([Multimodal Generative AI ch. 4](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch4)).

::: def
[Definition 9.10 — Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022)]{.tag} Train $\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c)$ on pairs $(x_0, c)$, where the condition $c$ is a class or a text prompt, and replace it by an empty token $\varnothing$ with probability about 10 %: one network learns both the conditional and the unconditional prediction.

At sampling, use in place of $\varepsilon_\theta$
$$
\tilde\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \varnothing) + w\,\big(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c) - \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \varnothing)\big).
$$
The weight $w = 1$ gives plain conditional sampling; $w > 1$ (7.5 by default in Stable Diffusion) pushes the samples towards the condition and trades diversity for fidelity, at the price of two network evaluations per step.
:::

The lab of session 12 trains a DDPM on a mixture of eight Gaussians in the plane, in a few minutes on a laptop CPU. Replacing the small MLP by a U-Net and the points by images gives an image DDPM; [Graph ML ch. 9](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9) transposes the same idea to graphs.

```python
import math, torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
def mixture(n):                                   # 8 Gaussians on the circle of radius 2
    a = 2 * math.pi * torch.randint(0, 8, (n,)) / 8
    return 2 * torch.stack([a.cos(), a.sin()], 1) + 0.1 * torch.randn(n, 2)

T = 200                                           # steps t = 0..T-1 in code, 1..T in the text
beta = torch.linspace(1e-4, 0.08, T); alpha = 1 - beta; abar = torch.cumprod(alpha, 0)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 128), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(128, 2))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
eps_hat = lambda x, t: net(torch.cat([x, t.float().unsqueeze(1) / T], 1))   # epsilon_theta(x_t, t)

for step in range(5000):                          # training: a plain regression on the noise
    x0 = mixture(256); t = torch.randint(0, T, (256,)); eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    a = abar[t].unsqueeze(1)
    xt = a.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - a).sqrt() * eps     # closed form (proposition 9.8)
    loss = ((eps - eps_hat(xt, t))**2).mean()     # noise-prediction loss
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

with torch.no_grad():                             # ancestral sampling (algorithm 9.9): T network calls
    x = torch.randn(2000, 2)
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        e = eps_hat(x, torch.full((2000,), t))
        x = (x - beta[t] / (1 - abar[t]).sqrt() * e) / alpha[t].sqrt()
        if t > 0: x = x + beta[t].sqrt() * torch.randn_like(x)
r = x.norm(dim=1)                                 # about 96 % of the samples within 0.3 of the circle,
print(((r - 2).abs() < 0.3).float().mean())       # spread over the 8 modes (no mode collapse)
```

The four families side by side:

| Family | Principle | Sampling | In the program |
|---|---|---|---|
| VAE | ELBO, Gaussian latent | decoder from $z \sim \mathcal{N}$ | here 9.2; Multimodal GenAI |
| GAN | adversarial min-max | implicit, one pass | here 9.3; Multimodal GenAI |
| Diffusion | iterative noising/denoising | $T$ denoising steps (algorithm 9.9) | here 9.4; Multimodal GenAI ch. 3–4 |
| Autoregressive | modeling $\mathbb{P}(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ | token by token | LLMs (M2), Graph GenAI |

## 10. Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Lutzeyer, Zhu) {#ch10}

This chapter connects the course to the current research of three researchers of the DaSciM group: Michalis Vazirgiannis (responsible of the course on the sheet), Johannes Lutzeyer (in its teaching team) and Ye Zhu (not listed on the 2026–2027 sheet). All three topics are rooted in the previous chapters. The arXiv references are in the bibliography.

### 10.1. Michalis Vazirgiannis: from the "Graph of Words" to textual GNNs

::: ex
[Worked example — Graph of Words (Rousseau & Vazirgiannis, CIKM 2013)]{.tag} Each distinct term of a document becomes a node, and a sliding window of size $w$ links the terms that co-occur in it: the document becomes a small weighted graph, and the weight of a term becomes its centrality instead of its frequency (TW-IDF instead of TF-IDF). The construction, TW-IDF and keyword extraction by k-core are developed in [NLP ch. 9](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch9), the site's reference. For this course, it is the first building block of the program: *the data itself becomes a graph*, which the Graph ML module generalizes.
:::

::: note
[GNN lineage: texts, expressivity, generation]{.tag}

-   **Inductive text classification via GNNs** (Skianis, Rousseau & Vazirgiannis, ACL 2020): each *document* is its own word graph; a GNN applied to the document graph can then process words never seen at training time (inductivity) whereas TextGCN (Yao et al., AAAI 2019) built a single corpus graph.
-   **DGoW-GNN** (Abbahaddou, Lutzeyer & Vazirgiannis, NeurIPS 2023): *discriminative* word graphs — the edges are no longer fixed co-occurrences but are filtered/learned for the task, then a GNN propagates the representations. The loop is closed with chapter 2: the computation graph (backprop) and the data graph (message passing) answer each other.
-   **PathNN** (Michel, Nikolentzos & Vazirgiannis, ICML 2023): going beyond classical message passing by aggregating *paths* (shortest paths, simple paths) emanating from each node; two variants are strictly more expressive than the Weisfeiler–Lehman test. This is the language of the Graph ML module, expanded in Advanced GNN (M2).
:::

### 10.2. Johannes Lutzeyer: where are the parameters? Expressivity and position

::: note
[Sparsifying the update step (Lutzeyer, Wu & Vazirgiannis, 2021)]{.tag} An MPNN (message passing neural network) chains two phases: the aggregation of neighbor messages and an "update step" — precisely the linear transformation + non-linearity of chapter 1, applied node by node. The paper's question: what remains if one *sparsifies* this trainable step, initializing it directly sparse (ExpanderGNN, with a tunable sparsity rate) or even reducing it to a non-linearity alone (Activation-Only GNN)?

Key result: performance comparable to dense models with far fewer parameters — a direct empirical insight into how expressivity is distributed between aggregation (structure, not parametrized) and the update (parametrized), in the spirit of ch. 1 (what, in a network, carries the expressivity?).
:::

::: note
[Positional encodings on graphs (SHAKE-GNN, Cui, Lutzeyer et al., 2025)]{.tag} Chapter 6 showed that a transformer needs a positional *encoding* because attention is permutation-invariant. On a graph, the problem is deeper: there is *no canonical ordering* of the nodes — the "position" of a node is a *structural* notion (Laplacian spectrum, distances, spanning forests). SHAKE-GNN proposes hierarchical encodings based on Kirchhoff forests, computed in a scalable way. The parallel to remember: RoPE (relative absolute position, suited to sequences) vs spectral/structural encodings (position defined by the geometry of the graph); both answer the same fundamental invariance (exercise 4). The Advanced GNN module (M2) systematizes this question.
:::

### 10.3. Ye Zhu: steering diffusion models

::: note
[From the loss to semantic control]{.tag} Section 9.4 set up the noising process, the noise-prediction loss and classifier-free guidance; the work of Ye Zhu shows how to *steer* diffusion further:

-   **BoundaryDiffusion** (Zhu et al., NeurIPS 2023): control the semantics of generation *without retraining* (learning-free), by warping the decision boundaries of the model's latent space in the guidance plane — an elegant point of contact with theorem 9.6: where the GAN sought an equilibrium, here already-learned latent regions are moved geometrically.
-   **Discrete contrastive diffusion** (ICLR 2023) and **Diffusion in Diffusion** (ICLR 2024): *discrete* cross-modal music-image diffusion and cyclic text-vision conditioning — the argument of the ch. 9 table ("multimodal") made concrete.
-   **NoiseQuery** (ICCV 2025): the initial noise $z_T$ as an *implicit control signal* for goal-guided generation — it reverses the perspective: the "noise" becomes a structured input, which connects to the sensitivity to the initial noise studied for GANs/diffusion.

This work directly extends ch. 9 and is expanded in the Multimodal Generative AI module.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Backprop on paper.** Recover the formulas of example 2.2 (two layers, ReLU), then check them numerically by finite differences
    $$
    \frac{\mathcal{L}(\theta + \epsilon e_j) - \mathcal{L}(\theta - \epsilon e_j)}{2\epsilon}
    $$
    on a small network.
2.  **★ Activation.** Show that if $\sigma$ is linear, an MLP of arbitrary depth represents exactly the affine maps. Deduce why *linear cascades* are useless.
3.  **★ 1D attention by hand.** For $n = 3$ tokens, $d_k = 2$, compute by hand $QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$, the row-wise softmax, and the result $\mathrm{softmax}(\cdot)V$. Implement it, compare, and check that the rows of the attention matrix sum to 1.
4.  **★ Permutation-equivariance.** Check experimentally that a transformer block *without* positional encoding is equivariant to the permutation of tokens (permuting the inputs permutes the outputs), and that adding a positional encoding breaks this equivariance.
5.  **★ Quadratic SGD.** Take $A = \mathrm{diag}(4, 1)$, $b = 0$, $\theta_0 = (1, 1)$.

    Write the sequence $(\theta_k)$ for $\eta = 1/2$ then $\eta = 1$, and verify theorem 3.1 (per-mode contraction, bound $2/L$).
6.  **★ Convolution arithmetic.** A $32 \times 32$ input, three successive convs (5×5, stride 2, padding 2; 3×3, stride 1, padding 1; 3×3, stride 1, padding 1, dilation 2): intermediate output sizes and final receptive field (proposition 4.4).
7.  **★ LoRA.** Count the trainable parameters of a GPT-like model with 12 blocks ($d = 768$, attention + MLP) adapted by LoRA $r = 8$ on the attention projections only, and compare with full fine-tuning.
8.  **★★ He initialization.** Recover the factor 2 of He initialization: for $h = \mathrm{ReLU}(a)$ with $a$ symmetric zero-mean, compute $\mathbb{E}[h^2]$ then the variance of the next layer.
9.  **★★ Adam bias correction.** Prove proposition 3.5 for $v_t$ (second moment), then compute the update $\hat m_1/\sqrt{\hat v_1}$ at the first step and explain why the warmup protects.
10. **★★ Gaussian KL.** Derive the formula of proposition 9.4 in dimension 1, plot
    $$
    \mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \| \mathcal{N}(0,1))
    $$
    as a function of $\mu$ and $\sigma$, and locate the minimum.
11. **★★ Gaussian GAN.** For $p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $p_G = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, write the logit of $D^\star$ (difference of the log-densities) and check that it is a trinomial in $x$. Where does the equilibrium lie?
12. **★★★ Project.** In PyTorch: classify MNIST with (a) an MLP, (b) a small CNN, (c) a mini-transformer on patches (16 patches of 4×4). Plot the train/val curves, compare the parameter counts and accuracy, comment with the bias-variance decomposition, then apply the protocol of chapter 8 (overfitting a batch, LR range test). (d) Train the CNN of (b) on the digits 0–4 only, freeze it, and train a linear classifier on its features for the digits 5–9 (linear probing, section 7.1); compare with the same CNN trained from scratch on 5–9.

::: note
[Solutions (Ex. 2, 3, 5, 6, 11) and hints (the others)]{.tag}

-   **Ex. 1.** Take $\epsilon \sim 10^{-6}$ in float64 for the check; the error of the central finite difference is $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)$.
-   **Ex. 2.** By induction: if
    $$
    h^{(\ell)} = \sigma(W^{(\ell)} h^{(\ell-1)} + b^{(\ell)})
    $$
    with $\sigma(t) = \alpha t$, then
    $$
    h^{(\ell)} = \alpha W^{(\ell)} h^{(\ell-1)} + \alpha b^{(\ell)}
    $$
    remains affine in $h^{(0)} = x$ — composing, $f_\theta(x) = W x + c$ with $W = \prod_\ell \alpha W^{(\ell)}$: a single matrix, all the deep layers collapse into one.
-   **Ex. 3.** The row-wise softmax makes each row a vector of positive weights of sum 1; the multiplication by $V$ makes each output a weighted average of the *values*: this is a convex interpolation, exactly the message passing of chapter 6.
-   **Ex. 4.** Permute the rows of the input batch ($x[\mathrm{perm}]$) and check that the output rows are permuted in the same way: the property (permutation equivariance) is exact (not an approximation), the softmax being unchanged by re-indexing.
-   **Ex. 5.** Decoupled modes: $(\theta_k)_1 = (1 - 4\eta)^k$, $(\theta_k)_2 = (1-\eta)^k$.

    For $\eta = 1/2$: factors $-1$ (oscillation without decay: exactly $\eta = 2/L$, limiting case) and $1/2$.

    For $\eta = 1$: factors $-3$ (divergence: $\eta > 2/L$) and $0$ (convergence in one step: $\eta = 1/\lambda_2$).
-   **Ex. 6.** Theorem 4.2: $32 \to 16 \to 16 \to 14$ (the third one: $\lfloor (16 + 2 - 2\cdot 2 - 1)/1 \rfloor + 1 = 14$).

    Receptive field (proposition 4.4, with dilation: replace $(k-1)$ by $d(k-1)$): $\mathrm{RF}_1 = 5$, $\mathrm{RF}_2 = 5 + 2 \cdot 2 = 9$, $\mathrm{RF}_3 = 9 + (2 \cdot 2)\cdot 2 = 17$ pixels, for a product of strides $\prod s = 2$.
-   **Ex. 7.** Per block: 4 attention matrices $d \times d$, i.e. $4 \times 2 \times 8 \times 768 = 49{,}152$ LoRA parameters, versus $4 \times 768^2 \approx 2.36$ M for full — and the MLP is not adapted; LoRA total \~0.6 M for \~85 M full.
-   **Ex. 8.** By symmetry of $a$,
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[h^2] = \mathbb{E}[a^2 \mathbf{1}_{a>0}] = \tfrac12\mathbb{E}[a^2]:
    $$
    the variance of the next layer is halved, hence $\mathrm{Var}(W) = 2/n_{\mathrm{in}}$.
-   **Ex. 9.** Re-derive the geometric sum with $g_k^2$ constant; at step 1, $\hat m_1 = g_1$ and $\hat v_1 = g_1^2$.

    The ratio is $\mathrm{sign}(g_1)$, a step of size $\eta$ whether $g_1$ is tiny or huge: hence the caution of the warmup when $g_1$ is atypical.
-   **Ex. 10.** The minimum of $\tfrac12(\mu^2 + \sigma^2 - 1 - \log\sigma^2)$ is reached at $\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$ (derivative with respect to $\sigma^2$: $\tfrac12(1 - 1/\sigma^2) = 0$).
-   **Ex. 11.** Unique global minimum at $(\mu, \sigma) = (0, 1)$; the logit of $D^\star$ is
    $$
    \frac{x^2}{2}\big(\frac{1}{\sigma^2} - 1\big) - \frac{x\mu}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log\sigma:
    $$
    a trinomial in $x$, identically zero at the equilibrium $(\mu, \sigma) = (0, 1)$.
:::

### A classical assessment {#projects-exam}

Since the sheet displays no mode for LLGA, this is a balanced default: a written exam on the chapters taught in class, two lab notebooks, and one project that extends Ex. 12 or follows a card below.

| Component | Weight | Format | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Written exam | 50 % | 2 h, no documents, one handwritten A4 sheet; the few numerical values needed are given | ch. 0–9 (in class), not the self-study ch. 10 |
| Lab notebooks | 20 % | two notebooks, 10 % each, handed in one week after the session | session 8 (gradient norm through time); session 11 or 12 (the VAE of 9.2 or the DDPM of 9.4) |
| Project | 30 % | Ex. 12 or one card below; report and 10-minute oral | started in session 10, due two weeks after session 12 |

**Resit.** A 2 h written exam of the same format replaces the exam grade; the lab and project grades are kept.

**Sample questions.** Five questions worth 20 points make a 2 h paper: two hand computations, one derivation, one computation with its interpretation, and one diagnosis.

**Q1 (4 pts) — Backpropagation by hand.** Take
$$
\mathcal{L}(w_1, w_2) = \tfrac12\big(w_2\,\mathrm{ReLU}(w_1 x) - t\big)^2, \qquad x = 2,\ t = 1,\ w_1 = 0.5,\ w_2 = -1.
$$
(a) Run the forward pass and give the loss. (b) Compute both partial derivatives with the recursion of theorem 2.1. (c) Take one gradient step with step size $0.1$ and give the new loss. (d) What are the gradients if $w_1 = -0.5$, and what does this predict for training?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) $a = w_1 x = 1$, $h = 1$, $y = -1$, loss $2$ (1 pt).
- (b) $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y = y - t = -2$, so $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_2 = -2h = -2$; the message $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h = (y - t)w_2 = 2$ crosses the ReLU (derivative $1$ at $a = 1$), and $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_1 = 2x = 4$ (1.5 pts).
- (c) $w_1 = 0.5 - 0.4 = 0.1$ and $w_2 = -1 + 0.2 = -0.8$; then $y = -0.8 \times 0.2 = -0.16$ and the loss falls from $2$ to $\tfrac12(1.16)^2 \approx 0.67$ (1 pt).
- (d) $a = -1 < 0$, so $h = 0$ and both gradients vanish: a dead ReLU, the row "neither train nor val moves" of table 8.2 (0.5 pt). Common error: forgetting the factor $x = \partial a/\partial w_1$.
:::

**Q2 (3 pts) — Convolution arithmetic.** An input of size $3 \times 64 \times 64$ goes through (1) a $7 \times 7$ convolution with 64 filters, stride 2, padding 3; (2) a $3 \times 3$ max-pooling, stride 2, padding 1; (3) a $3 \times 3$ convolution with 64 filters, stride 1, padding 1. (a) Give the spatial size after each layer. (b) Give the receptive field of one unit of layer 3, treating the pooling as a layer of kernel 3 and stride 2. (c) Count the parameters of layer 1, biases included.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Theorem 4.2: $\lfloor (64 + 6 - 6 - 1)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 32$, then $\lfloor (32 + 2 - 2 - 1)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 16$, then $16$ (1 pt).
- (b) Proposition 4.4: $7$, then $7 + 2 \times 2 = 11$, then $11 + 2 \times (2 \times 2) = 19$ pixels (1 pt). Common error: multiplying by the stride of the current layer instead of the product of the previous ones.
- (c) $7 \times 7 \times 3 \times 64 + 64 = 9\,472$ (1 pt).
:::

**Q3 (4 pts) — Attention by hand.** One query and two keys and values, with $d_k = 4$:
$$
q = (1, 1, 1, 1), \quad k_1 = (1, 1, 1, 1), \quad k_2 = (1, -1, 1, -1), \quad v_1 = (1, 0), \quad v_2 = (0, 1).
$$
Use $e^2 \approx 7.39$ and $e^4 \approx 54.6$.

(a) Compute the scaled scores, the attention weights and the output. (b) Redo the weights without the $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling and explain, with proposition 6.2, why the unscaled form fails in high dimension. (c) The query is the first token of a causal model and $k_2$ belongs to the second token: what are the weights and the output?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Scores $q^\top k_j/2 = (2, 0)$; weights $(7.39, 1)/8.39 \approx (0.881, 0.119)$; output $0.881\,v_1 + 0.119\,v_2 = (0.881, 0.119)$ (1.5 pts).
- (b) Scores $(4, 0)$ and weights $\approx (0.982, 0.018)$, close to one-hot. With unit-variance coordinates the score variance is $d_k$, so its standard deviation is $\sqrt{d_k}$ (32 for $d_k = 1024$); the softmax saturates and its gradient $\hat y_k(\delta_{kj} - \hat y_j)$ vanishes (1.5 pts).
- (c) The mask sets the score of the future token to $-\infty$: weights $(1, 0)$, output $v_1 = (1, 0)$ (1 pt). Common error: normalising over columns instead of rows.
:::

**Q4 (5 pts) — Diffusion in one page.** (a) From definition 9.7, prove proposition 9.8 for $t = 2$.

(b) With $\beta_1 = 0.1$ and $\beta_2 = 0.2$, give $\bar\alpha_2$ and the coefficients of the data point and of the noise in $x_2$ (use $\sqrt{0.72} \approx 0.85$ and $\sqrt{0.28} \approx 0.53$).

(c) Write the noise-prediction loss and explain why a training step needs one network evaluation while sampling needs $T$. (d) Write the classifier-free guidance combination and say what the weight $w$ trades.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Substitute the first step into the second:
    $$
    x_2 = \sqrt{\alpha_2}\,\big(\sqrt{\alpha_1}\,x_0 + \sqrt{\beta_1}\,\varepsilon_1\big) + \sqrt{\beta_2}\,\varepsilon_2 = \sqrt{\alpha_1\alpha_2}\,x_0 + \sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}\,\varepsilon_1 + \sqrt{\beta_2}\,\varepsilon_2 ;
    $$
    the noise is a sum of independent centred Gaussians of variance $\alpha_2(1 - \alpha_1) + 1 - \alpha_2 = 1 - \alpha_1\alpha_2$ (2 pts).
- (b) $\bar\alpha_2 = 0.9 \times 0.8 = 0.72$, so $x_2 \approx 0.85\,x_0 + 0.53\,\varepsilon$; check $0.8 \times 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.28$ (1 pt).
- (c) The loss of section 9.4: thanks to the closed form, one draws $t$, $\varepsilon$ and $x_t$ directly and makes one regression step; sampling runs algorithm 9.9 from $x_T$, one evaluation per step (1 pt).
- (d) Definition 9.10: $w = 1$ is conditional sampling, $w > 1$ gives samples more faithful to the condition and less diverse, at two evaluations per step (1 pt). Common error: confusing $\alpha_t$ with $\bar\alpha_t$.
:::

**Q5 (4 pts) — Diagnosing two runs.** Run A: an MLP trained with Adam; the training loss falls from 2.3 to 0.05 in 20 epochs, the validation loss reaches 0.40 at epoch 8 and then rises to 0.70. Run B: the same model with a learning rate of $10^{-1}$ instead of $10^{-3}$ and fp16 mixed precision; the loss is NaN from step 300, and the gradient norm jumped just before.

(a) Name the phenomenon of run A and give three remedies in order of payoff. (b) Give two likely causes of run B, with the response to each. (c) Which check of the recipe of section 8.1 should precede both runs, and what does it detect?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Overfitting: the train/validation gap opens while the training loss falls (1 pt). Remedies in the order of the note of section 3.6: more data, augmentation, dropout, weight decay; stopping at epoch 8 is accepted as early stopping (1 pt).
- (b) A step beyond the stability edge $2/L$ of theorem 3.1: divide the learning rate by 10, add warmup or clipping; an fp16 overflow or an unprotected softmax or log: bf16 or loss scaling, log-softmax (1 pt).
- (c) Overfitting a single batch of 32 examples, which detects structural bugs, or the LR range test, which sets the learning rate; either is accepted with its justification (1 pt). Common error: "train longer" for run A.
:::

### Projects {#projects-list}

House rules: public data, a laptop CPU or one free Colab T4 GPU, and only what this module, the Machine Learning module of the same period and the refreshers teach. Levels ★, ★★ and ★★★ mean what they mean for the exercises; effort per student is 8–15 h for ★, 15–25 h for ★★ and 25–35 h for ★★★.

**Grading grid used by every project of this page** (a project card may replace one row).

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Question and success metric stated before the experiments | 10 % |
| Correct use of the course results (cited by number) | 25 % |
| Protocol: leakage-free split, baselines, at least 3 seeds, intervals | 25 % |
| Results and analysis: error analysis, limits, one responsible-AI remark | 20 % |
| Reproducibility: repository, README, pinned environment, one command | 10 % |
| Communication: report (≤ 6 pages solo, ≤ 10 group) or 10-minute oral | 10 % |

Group projects: a contribution statement and an oral with individual questions; the individual grade is the group grade times a factor in [0.8, 1.2].

#### P1 · ★ · solo · Controlled-bug study of the training recipe {#proj-1}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Inject four bugs into a working Fashion-MNIST CNN (learning rate ×100, all-zero initialization, `-log(softmax)` computed in float16, 1,000 training images without regularization) and show, over 3 seeds each, whether the symptom predicted by table 8.2 appears and whether the listed response brings test accuracy back within 1 point of the clean baseline. |
| Data | [Fashion-MNIST](https://github.com/zalandoresearch/fashion-mnist) — MIT licence — 70,000 grey images of 28 × 28 pixels, 10 classes; loading: `torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST("data", train=True, download=True)` |
| Chapters | [ch. 0](#ch0) (0.3 stable softmax), [ch. 1](#ch1) (1.3 initialization), [ch. 3](#ch3) (theorem 3.1, 3.6), [ch. 8](#ch8) (8.1 recipe, 8.2 symptom table) |
| Deliverables | notebook + 4-page report with one table: bug × seed × (symptom observed, step at which it is detected, accuracy after the fix) |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 12 h · laptop CPU, about 15 runs, longest run ≤ 5 min |
| Objectives served | O1 (optimisation and stability), O7 (debugging practice) |
| Specific criterion | Replaces "Correct use of the course results" (25 %): each bug is tied to the result that predicts its symptom (theorem 3.1, proposition 0.3, the note on zero initialization in 1.3, the note of 3.6). |
| Going further | Add 20 % label noise as a fifth bug and explain why the overfit-one-batch check of 8.1 does not catch it. |

#### P2 · ★★ · solo · Label-efficient medical images (extends Ex. 12) {#proj-2}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Measure test accuracy on PathMNIST (and macro-F1 on DermaMNIST) at 100, 1,000 and 10,000 labelled images for an MLP, a small CNN and the mini-transformer of Ex. 12 trained from scratch, and for an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 used as a linear probe and fully fine-tuned; report the label count above which transfer no longer beats the CNN baseline. |
| Data | [MedMNIST v2](https://medmnist.com/) — PathMNIST CC BY 4.0 (107,180 colon-pathology patches, 9 classes), DermaMNIST CC BY-NC 4.0 (10,015 dermatoscopic images, 7 classes), 28 × 28 pixels; loading: `pip install medmnist`, then `medmnist.PathMNIST(split="train", download=True)` |
| Chapters | [ch. 3](#ch3), [ch. 4](#ch4), [ch. 6](#ch6) (6.4), [ch. 7](#ch7) (7.1 regimes), [ch. 8](#ch8); extends [Ex. 12](#ex) |
| Deliverables | notebook + 4-page report with the accuracy-versus-labels curves, 3 seeds per point, intervals |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 20 h · one free Colab T4, longest run ≤ 20 min (images upsampled to 64 × 64 for the ResNet) |
| Objectives served | O6 (health imaging), O7 (transfer-learning practice) |
| Responsible AI | DermaMNIST is non-commercial, and its source (HAM10000) contains mostly light skin: report per-class recall, state that no audit by skin type is possible, and make no clinical claim. |
| Going further | The 224 × 224 MedMNIST+ images, or LoRA (7.3) on the attention projections of a small pretrained vision transformer. |

#### P3 · ★★ · solo · LoRA versus linear probe versus full fine-tuning {#proj-3}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | On Amazon Polarity (20,000 training reviews) and PubMedQA, compare a linear probe on frozen DistilBERT features (the baseline), LoRA with rank 4, 8 and 16 on the attention projections, and full fine-tuning: accuracy, trainable parameters (checked against the count of Ex. 7) and GPU minutes. |
| Data | [Amazon Polarity](https://huggingface.co/datasets/fancyzhx/amazon_polarity) — Apache 2.0 — 3.6 M reviews, of which a 20,000 / 5,000 subset; [PubMedQA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/qiaojin/PubMedQA) — MIT — the 1,000 expert-labelled questions with their abstracts (yes / no / maybe), 5-fold cross-validation; loading: `datasets.load_dataset("qiaojin/PubMedQA", "pqa_labeled")` |
| Chapters | [ch. 6](#ch6) (6.5 masked language models), [ch. 7](#ch7) (7.1, 7.3 LoRA), [ch. 8](#ch8); [Ex. 7](#ex) |
| Deliverables | notebook + 4-page report with one table per dataset: method × accuracy (mean ± std over 3 seeds) × trainable parameters × GPU minutes × peak memory |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 18 h · one free Colab T4, longest run ≤ 30 min (one epoch of full fine-tuning on 20,000 reviews) |
| Objectives served | O3 (transformers and fine-tuning), O6 (biomedical text), O7 (cost-aware engineering) |
| Responsible AI | The reviews were written by people: no attempt to identify authors; PubMedQA answers summarise research conclusions and are not medical advice. |
| Going further | QLoRA on a 0.5B decoder (the PEFT box of [LLMs ch. 4](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch4)). |

#### P4 · ★★★ · group (3–4) · A character VAE for molecules {#proj-4}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Train a SMILES character VAE (GRU encoder and decoder) and report the validity, uniqueness and novelty of 10,000 samples (RDKit) and the reconstruction accuracy, against a character-level GRU language model sampled token by token as baseline; show latent interpolations between two molecules. |
| Data | [ZINC250k through TDC](https://tdcommons.ai/generation_tasks/molgen/) — ZINC terms: free to use for everyone, redistribution of significant subsets needs the authors' permission (download it, do not commit it) — 249,455 molecules; loading: `from tdc.generation import MolGen; MolGen(name="ZINC")` |
| Chapters | [ch. 5](#ch5) (GRU, teacher forcing), [ch. 9](#ch9) (9.2 ELBO and reparameterization), [ch. 8](#ch8) |
| Deliverables | repository with a one-command run, README and pinned environment + report of at most 10 pages + 10-minute oral with individual questions |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 30 h per student · one free Colab T4, longest run ≤ 2 h |
| Objectives served | O2 (hands-on generative models), O6 (pharma and molecules) |
| Specific criterion | Replaces "Protocol" (25 %): KL annealing, a posterior-collapse diagnosis (KL per latent dimension), 3 seeds, metrics on 10,000 samples. |
| Responsible AI | Dual use: the generated molecules are not screened for toxicity and no synthesis route is proposed; the report states this limit. |
| Going further | A diffusion model (9.4) on the VAE codes, or the graph generators of [Graph ML ch. 9](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9) in Period 2. |

### End-of-year projects {#projects-capstone}

For students who take Deep Learning in Period 1, this course supplies the deep-learning component of every Year-1 integrative project, for instance the transformer encoder of [Y1-5](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-5) (ch. 6), the GRU generator of [Y1-6](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-6) (ch. 5 and 9; card P4 prepares it), the CNN and transfer learning of [Y1-7](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-7) (ch. 4 and 7; card P2 prepares it) and the LoRA retriever variant of [Y1-8](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-8) (ch. 7).

In Year 2, the SELFIES decoder of capstone [C3](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c3) (ch. 6; section 9.4 for guidance and for its DiGress baseline) and the permutation-equivariant attention of [C6](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c6) (ch. 6) build on it.
